source.title: Symmetry and colorings: some results and open problems, II

accepted.question_text: Let X be a compact subset of R^n with positive Lebesgue measure, where n > 2, and let ms_r(X) denote the largest measure that is guaranteed for a monochromatic symmetric subset in every measurable r-coloring of X. Classify the numbers ms_r(X) for such sets X. In particular, determine ms_r(X) for every regular convex polyhedron in R^n with n > 2, and determine ms_2(T) for the regular tetrahedron T in R^3.
accepted.context_brief: Maximal symmetry numbers in higher-dimensional Euclidean space

evidence.quote: For such a triple X = (X, µ, S) (called a symmetry measure space) we shall evaluate the maximal symmetry numbers msr(X) equal to the maximal measure of a symmetric subset that can be found in each measurable r-coloring of X.

Problem 5.4. Classify maximal symmetry numbers msr(X) of compact subsets X of positive Lebesgue measure in Rn for n > 2. In particular, calculate msr(X) for all regular convex polyhedra X in Rn for n > 2. Calculate ms2(T ) (or equivalently, ms2(S4 × I)) for the regular tetrahedron T in R3.

accepted.question_text: For the sphere S^n, let S^+_2 be the family of non-identity involutive orientation-preserving isometries, that is, 180-degree rotations about lines through the center. Is ms_r(S^n, S^+_2) = 1/r^2 for all n, r > 1? Equivalently, does every measurable r-coloring of S^n contain a monochromatic subset of measure at least 1/r^2 that is symmetric with respect to some line through the center of the sphere?
accepted.context_brief: Orientation-preserving involutions on spheres

evidence.quote: • S+2 is the family of non-identity involutive orientation-preserving isometries of X;

Question 5.6. Is msr(Sn, S+2 ) = 1/r2 for n, r > 1? More precisely, does for every measurable r-coloring of the n-dimensional sphere Sn there exist a monochromatic subset of measure ≥ 1/r2, symmetric with respect to some line passing through the center of the sphere?

accepted.question_text: For the finite interval n = {0, 1, ..., n-1} with counting measure and integer central symmetries, let bms_r(n) be the blurred maximal symmetry number obtained by taking the infimum over measurable blurred r-colorings. Calculate the values of bms_r(n), at least for small n and for r = 2.
accepted.context_brief: Blurred maximal symmetry numbers on finite intervals

evidence.quote: Taking this infimum over all measurable blurred r-colorings of X, we obtain the definition of the blurred maximal symmetry number bmsr(X).
Problem 6.3. Calculate the values bmsr(n) (at least for small n and r = 2).

accepted.question_text: Let I = [0,1] be the unit interval with Lebesgue measure and the family of central symmetries s_c(x) = 2c - x. Calculate the maximal symmetry numbers ms_r(I), at least in the first nontrivial case r = 2.
accepted.context_brief: Maximal symmetry numbers of the unit interval

evidence.quote: In this section we consider one of the most difficult and challenging open problems related to our subject — evaluating the maximal symmetry numbers msr(I) for the unit interval I = [0, 1] in the real line R endowed with the Lebesgue measure µ and the family S = {sc : c ∈ R} of central symmetries sc : x 7→ 2c − x.
Problem 6.4. Calculate the values msr(I) (at least for r = 2).

accepted.question_text: Let I = [0,1] be the unit interval with Lebesgue measure and central symmetries x ↦ 2c − x. Let ms_r(I) be the maximal symmetry number for measurable r-colorings of I, meaning the largest measure guaranteed for a monochromatic measurable subset that is symmetric about some center c. In the asymptotic formula lim_{r→∞} r^2 · ms_r(I) = inf_{r∈N} r^2 · ms_r(I) = S', determine or estimate the constant S'. Decide whether S' is strictly larger than the constant S from the autoconvolution lower bound for ms_r(I).
accepted.context_brief: Asymptotic constant for interval symmetry numbers

evidence.quote: The exact value of the constant S is not known.
(6) limr→∞ r2 · msr(I) = infr∈N r2 · msr(I) = S′ for some constant S′ such that S ≤ S′ < 5/6;
Problem 6.5. Calculate or evaluate the constant S′ from Theorem 6.2(6). Is S′ > S?

accepted.question_text: How quickly do the sequences {ms_r(n)/n}_{n=1}^∞ and {bms_r(n)/n}_{n=1}^∞ converge to their common limit ms_r(I) = bms_r(I)?
accepted.context_brief: Convergence rate from discrete to continuous interval symmetry numbers

evidence.quote: (1) msr(I) = limn→∞ msr(n)/n = infn∈N msr(n)/n;
(2) bmsr(I) = limn→∞ bmsr(n)/n = infn∈N bmsr(n)/n;
Problem 6.6. How quickly do the sequences {msr(n)/n}∞n=1 and {bmsr(n)/n}∞n=1 converge to their limit msr(I) = bmsr(I)?

accepted.question_text: Fix an integer r ≥ 1. For a compact Abelian group G with Haar measure and central symmetries s_c(x) = c x^{-1} c, determine exactly which groups satisfy ms_r(G) = 1/r^2.
accepted.context_brief: Compact Abelian groups with extremal symmetry number

evidence.quote: Each group G will be endowed with the family of admissible symmetries S = {sc : c ∈ G} containing involutive transformations sc : x 7→ cx−1c, called central symmetries of the group G.
Problem 7.4. Given an integer number r, detect Abelian groups G with msr(G) = 1/r2.

accepted.question_text: For a finite group G of odd order, is the maximal symmetry number always strictly larger than 1/r^2 for every r > 1?
accepted.context_brief: Odd-order finite groups

evidence.quote: Theorem 7.6. Each finite Abelian group G of odd cardinality has the maximal symmetry numbers msr(G) = m˜sr(G) > 1/r2 for all finite r ≥ 2.
Question 7.7. Is msr(G) > 1/r2 for every group G of odd order and every r > 1?

accepted.question_text: Given ε > 0 and an integer r > 1, does there exist a finite group G whose maximal symmetry number ms_r(G) is smaller than ε?
accepted.context_brief: How small finite-group symmetry numbers can be

evidence.quote: Surprisingly, but for non-commutative groups of even order the inequality msr(G) ≥ 1/r2 does not hold anymore: it was noticed in [6] that msr(Q8) = 1/8 < 1/22, where Q8 = {±1, ±i, ±j, ±k} is the group of quaternions.
Question 7.8 ([6]). Does for every ε > 0 and r > 1 there exist a finite group G with msr(G) < ε?

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a connected compact group G for which ms_r(G) < 1/r^2 for some integer r? In particular, what are the exact values of ms_2(SO(3)) and of ms_2(S^3), where S^3 is the multiplicative group of unit quaternions?
accepted.context_brief: Connected compact groups

evidence.quote: Theorem 7.10 ([7]). If r ∈ N and G is a non-degenerate connected compact group, then 1/r2 · 1/2dim G ≤ msr(G) ≤ 1/r2.

Question 7.11 ([7]). Is there a connected compact group G with msr(G) < 1/r2 for some r ∈ N? In particular, what is the value of ms2(SO(3))? What is the value of ms2(S3) where S3 is the multiplicative group of quaternions with unit norm?

accepted.question_text: Let G be an infinite group, and let MS_r(G) and MS_r^+(G) be the cardinal symmetry numbers defined using central symmetries and the cardinal-valued measures card and card^+. Must both MS_r(G) and MS_r^+(G) be infinite for every finite number of colors r? Equivalently, does every finite coloring of an infinite group contain monochromatic symmetric subsets of arbitrarily large finite size?
accepted.context_brief: Cardinal symmetry numbers of infinite groups

evidence.quote: We shall be interested in the maximal symmetry numbers msr(G, card, S) and msr(G, card+, S) of groups G endowed with the family S = {sc : c ∈ G} of central symmetries sc : x 7→ cx−1c. These symmetry Ramsey numbers will be denoted by MSr(G) and MS+r(G), respectively, and will be referred to as cardinal symmetry numbers of G.

Problem 8.4 (Protasov). Are the cardinals MSr(G) and MS+r(G) infinite for every infinite group G and every finite cardinal r? Equivalently, is it true that for every finite coloring of an infinite group G there exist a monochromatic symmetric subset A ⊂ G of arbitrary large finite cardinality?

accepted.question_text: Let G = SL(K), where K is an infinite field. Is the cardinal symmetry number MS_r^+(G) equal to |G|^+ for every finite number of colors r?
accepted.context_brief: Cardinal symmetry numbers of special linear groups

evidence.quote: Example 8.7. For any infinite field K of characteristic 6= 2, the special linear group G = SL(K) has cardinal symmetry number MS+2 (G) = |G|+, which means that for any 2-coloring of the group G = SL(K) there is a monochromatic symmetric subset of cardinality |G|.
Problem 8.8. Let G = SL(K) for an infinite field K. Is MS+r(G) = |G|+ for all finite cardinals r?

accepted.question_text: For the free group F_2 on two generators, is the cardinal symmetry number MS_r^+(F_2) uncountable for every finite number of colors r?
accepted.context_brief: Cardinal symmetry numbers of the free group F2

evidence.quote: Theorem 8.15 implies that the free group F2 with two generators has uncountable cardinal symmetry number MS+2 (F2), which means that for each 2-coloring of F2 there is an infinite monochromatic symmetric subset of F2.
Problem 8.18. Is MS+r(F2) uncountable for any finite cardinal r?

accepted.question_text: Let H^2 be the hyperbolic plane with the family of central symmetries s_c that reflect points through a midpoint c, and let mds_r(H^2) be the corresponding dimension symmetry number based on asymptotic dimension. Is mds_r(H^2) ≥ 0 for every r ≥ 2? Equivalently, does every r-coloring of H^2 contain an unbounded monochromatic symmetric subset?
accepted.context_brief: Dimension symmetry in the hyperbolic plane

evidence.quote: Since a subset A of a metric space X is unbounded if and only if asdim(A) ≥ 0, the space X has dimension symmetry number mdsBr(X) ≥ 0 if and only if for any Borel r-coloring, the space X contains an unbounded monochromatic S-symmetric subset.
Problem 9.3. Is mdsr(H2) ≥ 0 for any r ≥ 2?

accepted.question_text: Given a symmetry measure space X = (X, µ, S), a number of colors r, and a threshold λ in the measure range, calculate the (r, λ)-centerpole number c_r^λ(X), meaning the smallest size of a subfamily S' ⊂ S such that every measurable r-coloring of X contains a monochromatic S'-symmetric measurable set of measure at least λ.
accepted.context_brief: General centerpole numbers

evidence.quote: A subfamily S′ ⊂ S will be called (r, λ)-centerpole if for any measurable r-coloring of X there is a monochromatic S′-symmetric subset A ∈ dom(µ) of measure µ(A) ≥ λ. The minimal cardinality |S′| of a (r, λ)-centerpole subset S′ ⊂ S will be denoted by cλr (X) and called the (r, λ)-centerpole number of X.
Problem 10.1. Given a symmetry measure space X = (X, µ, S) calculate its (r, λ)-centerpole numbers cλr (X).

accepted.question_text: For Euclidean space R^n and the integer lattice Z^n, both equipped with central symmetries and asymptotic dimension, is it always true that c_r^0(R^n) = c_r^0(Z^n) for every r ≤ n? Here c_r^0 is the minimum number of centers needed to force an unbounded monochromatic symmetric subset in every r-coloring.
accepted.context_brief: Comparing Euclidean and lattice centerpole numbers

evidence.quote: Observe that for a symmetry measure space X = (X, µ, S) the centerpole number c0r(X) is equal to the smallest cardinality |S′| of a subfamily S′ ⊂ S such that for each r-coloring of X there is an unbounded monochromatic S′-symmetric subset A ⊂ X.
Problem 10.4. Is c0r(Rn) = c0r(Zn) for all r ≤ n?

accepted.question_text: Call a subset C ⊂ R^4 4-centerpole when the central symmetries with centers in C force an unbounded monochromatic symmetric subset under every 4-coloring. Is every 12-element 4-centerpole subset of R^4 affinely equivalent to the sandwich Ξ^3_1, the 12-point subset of Z^4 whose slices {-1} × 2^3_{<1}, {0} × 2^3_{<3}, and {1} × 2^3_{>1} have 1, 7, and 4 points, respectively?
accepted.context_brief: Structure of minimal 4-centerpole sets in R4

evidence.quote: We shall say that a subset C ⊂ Rn is r-centerpole if the family of central symmetries SC = {sc : c ∈ C} is (r, 0)-centerpole, which means that msr(Rn, asdim, SC ) ≥ 0.
• Ξ31 is a 12-element subset of Z4 whose slices {−1} × 23−1, {0} × 23<3 and {1} × 23>1 have 1, 7 and 4 points, respectively.
Problem 10.6. Is each 12-element 4-centerpole set in R4 affinely equivalent to the 31-sandwich Ξ31?

accepted.question_text: Determine the (5,0)-centerpole number c_5^0(R^5) for Euclidean 5-space, that is, the smallest number of centers needed to force an unbounded monochromatic symmetric subset in every 5-coloring of R^5. The known bounds are 18 ≤ c_5^0(R^5) ≤ c_5^0(Z^5) ≤ 25.
accepted.context_brief: Five-color centerpole number in R5

evidence.quote: Observe that for a symmetry measure space X = (X, µ, S) the centerpole number c0r(X) is equal to the smallest cardinality |S′| of a subfamily S′ ⊂ S such that for each r-coloring of X there is an unbounded monochromatic S′-symmetric subset A ⊂ X.
Problem 10.7. Calculate the (5,0)-centerpole number c05 (R5) of the Euclidean space R5. Theorem 10.3 yields the bounds 18 ≤ c05 (R5) ≤ c05 (Z5) ≤ 25.

accepted.question_text: What is the growth rate of the sequence {c_r^0(R^r)}_{r=1}^∞? Is it exponential or polynomial in r?
accepted.context_brief: Asymptotic growth of diagonal centerpole numbers

evidence.quote: Observe that the upper bound for c0r(Rr) in Theorem 10.3 has exponential growth while the lower bound has polynomial growth.
Problem 10.8. What is the growth of the sequence (c0r(Rr))∞r=1? Exponential or polynomial?

accepted.question_text: For Euclidean spaces R^n equipped with central symmetries, calculate or estimate the centerpole numbers c_r^λ(R^n) for various choices of the number of colors r, the threshold λ, and the dimension n.
accepted.context_brief: Centerpole numbers in Euclidean spaces

evidence.quote: The proof of Theorem 9.1 implies that c0r(Rn) ≤ cλr (Rn) < 2n for any finite nonnegative number r, λ, n with r + λ ≤ n + 1. So, we have some lower and upper bounds for the centerpole numbers cλr (Rn).
Problem 10.9. Calculate or evaluate the centerpole numbers cλr (Rn) for various numbers r, λ and n.

accepted.question_text: Given an (Abelian) group G viewed as the symmetry measure space (G, asdim, S) with central symmetries, calculate or estimate its dimension symmetry numbers mds_r(G).
accepted.context_brief: Dimension symmetry numbers of groups

evidence.quote: To shorten notations, by mdsr(G) we shall denote the maximal symmetry number msr(G, asdim, S) of the symmetry measure space (G, asdim, S) and call it the dimension symmetry number of G.
Problem 11.2. Given an (Abelian) group G calculate or evaluate its dimension symmetry numbers mdsr(G).

accepted.question_text: Given a group G viewed as the symmetry measure space (G, asdim, S) with central symmetries, calculate or estimate its centerpole numbers c_r^λ(G).
accepted.context_brief: Centerpole numbers of groups

evidence.quote: A similar problem can be asked for the centerpole numbers cλr (G) of the symmetry measure spaces (G, asdim, S).
Problem 11.3. Given a group G calculate or evaluate its centerpole numbers cλr (G).

accepted.question_text: Does the free group F_2 have finite centerpole numbers c_r^0(F_2) for every integer r?
accepted.context_brief: Centerpole finiteness for the free group F2

evidence.quote: Much less is known about the centerpole numbers of non-commutative groups, in particular, of the free group F2 with two generators.
Problem 11.4. Has the free group F2 finite centerpole numbers c0r(F2) for all r ∈ N?

accepted.question_text: For the free group F_2 on two generators, is the 2-color centerpole number c_2^0(F_2) equal to 4, 3, or 2?
accepted.context_brief: Exact two-color centerpole number for F2

evidence.quote: For r = 2 the answer to this problem is affirmative. Analyzing the proof of Theorem 1 of [29], one can see that c02 (F2) ≤ 4.
Problem 11.5. Is c02 (F2) equal to 4, 3, or 2?
